title: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9–1) History Specification
subtitle: Option 33: Conflict at Home and Abroad: the USA, 1954–75

sections.title: Key topic 1: The development of the civil rights movement, 1954–60

topics.title: The Position of Black Americans in the Early 1950s
points: **Racial segregation, social discrimination, and voting rights in Southern states.**
**The efforts and campaigns of civil rights groups, specifically the NAACP and CORE.**
topics.narrative_blurb: In the early 1950s, Black Americans endured systemic **racial segregation, social discrimination, and voting rights** denial across Southern states under brutal Jim Crow laws. Legal challenges spearheaded by the **NAACP** attacked the 'separate but equal' doctrine in the courts, while **CORE** pioneered non-violent direct action, organizing early sit-ins to challenge entrenched institutional racism.

topics.title: Progress in Education and Legal Challenges
points: **The causes, core features, and historical impact of the Brown v. Topeka ruling (1954).**
**The causes, key developments, and importance of the desegregation crisis at Little Rock Central High School (1957).**
topics.narrative_blurb: Thurgood Marshall secured a landmark triumph in **the Brown v. Topeka ruling (1954)**, where Chief Justice Warren declared segregated schooling inherently unequal. Southern white backlash erupted in **the desegregation crisis at Little Rock Central High School (1957)**, compelling President Eisenhower to federalize the National Guard and dispatch the 101st Airborne to escort the 'Little Rock Nine'.

topics.title: The Montgomery Bus Boycott and Its Impact
points: **The historical role and impact of Rosa Parks' activism.**
**The origins, course, and key events of the Montgomery Bus Boycott.**
**The importance of Martin Luther King Jr.'s leadership during the campaign.**
**The factors behind the boycott's success and its overall significance.**
**The ruling of the Supreme Court regarding bus segregation.**
**The establishment and goals of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC).**
topics.narrative_blurb: The courage of **Rosa Parks' activism** sparked the 381-day **Montgomery Bus Boycott**, demonstrating immense economic leverage. Elevated by **Martin Luther King Jr.'s leadership**, the movement achieved victory when the Supreme Court ruled segregated buses unconstitutional in Browder v. Gayle, cementing non-violent protest and inspiring the **establishment and goals of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC)**.

topics.title: Resistance to Civil Rights and the 1957 Act
points: **Resistance to desegregation in the South, focusing on the Dixiecrats and the formation of White Citizens' Councils.**
**Racial violence and the Ku Klux Klan, including the 1955 murder of Emmett Till.**
**The passage and effectiveness of the Civil Rights Act of 1957.**
topics.narrative_blurb: Desegregation triggered fierce Southern resistance led by conservative **Dixiecrats and the formation of White Citizens' Councils**. Terror intensified through **racial violence and the Ku Klux Klan**, underscored by the horrific **1955 murder of Emmett Till**. Although Congress enacted the **Civil Rights Act of 1957**, weak enforcement mechanisms severely limited its immediate practical impact on voter registration.

sections.title: Key topic 2: Protest, progress and radicalism, 1960–75

topics.title: Progress 1960–62: Sit-ins and Freedom Rides
points: **The impact of the Greensboro sit-ins and the growth of the student movement.**
**The causes, key events, and impact of the Freedom Rides, including white supremacist violence and the Anniston bus bombing (1961).**
**The desegregation of the University of Mississippi and the James Meredith case (1962).**
topics.narrative_blurb: Youth activism surged through the **Greensboro sit-ins and the growth of the student movement**, founding SNCC. In 1961, CORE and SNCC tested interstate transit through **the Freedom Rides**, surviving the brutal **Anniston bus bombing (1961)**. Federal authority was asserted again in **the desegregation of the University of Mississippi and the James Meredith case (1962)** using federal troops.

topics.title: Birmingham, Washington and the Civil Rights Act 1964
points: **The 1963 non-violent campaigns led by Martin Luther King Jr. in Birmingham and Washington.**
**The Freedom Summer voter drive and the KKK murders of civil rights workers in Mississippi.**
**The effectiveness of non-violent activism and the contributions of Presidents Kennedy and Johnson to the Civil Rights Act of 1964.**
topics.narrative_blurb: Non-violent direct action reached its zenith through King's campaigns in **Birmingham and Washington**, televised globally. Overcoming the Mississippi **KKK murders of civil rights workers**, activism and the political leverage of **Presidents Kennedy and Johnson** culminated in the landmark **Civil Rights Act of 1964**, legally dismantling public segregation and employment discrimination across the nation.

topics.title: Selma, the Voting Rights Act 1965 and Malcolm X
points: **The Selma campaign, the Edmund Pettus Bridge attack, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.**
**Malcolm X's ideology, political methods, and work with the Nation of Islam.**
**His subsequent shift in philosophy and his 1965 assassination.**
topics.narrative_blurb: State violence on the **Edmund Pettus Bridge** during the Selma campaign prompted President Johnson to sign the transformative **Voting Rights Act of 1965**. Concurrently, Northern ghetto disillusionment amplified **Malcolm X's ideology** of Black nationalism and self-defense within the **Nation of Islam**, which persisted despite his philosophical moderation and tragic **1965 assassination**.

topics.title: Black Power, the Black Panthers and MLK Assassination
points: **The causes behind the rise of the Black Power movement in urban areas.**
**The role of Stokely Carmichael and the protest at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics.**
**The tactics, social programs, and achievements of the Black Panther Party.**
**Urban disturbances of 1965–67 and the findings of the 1968 Kerner Report.**
**The murder of Martin Luther King Jr. in 1968 and its national consequences.**
topics.narrative_blurb: Frustration with Northern economic deprivation fueled the **rise of the Black Power movement**, popularized by **Stokely Carmichael**, the **1968 Mexico City Olympics** salute, and the armed patrols and community **social programs of the Black Panther Party**. Following bloody **urban disturbances of 1965–67**, the devastating **murder of Martin Luther King Jr. in 1968** ignited riots across 100 cities.

sections.title: Key topic 3: US involvement in the Vietnam War, 1954–75

topics.title: Reasons for US Involvement in Vietnam, 1954–63
points: **Factors leading to increased US involvement under President Eisenhower, including the domino theory and Ngo Dinh Diem's administrative failures.**
**Escalation of US involvement under President Kennedy, focusing on the Strategic Hamlet Program and Ngo Dinh Diem's removal.**
topics.narrative_blurb: Cold War containment and the **domino theory** drove US intervention following the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu (1954) and the Geneva Accords. Presidents Eisenhower and Kennedy provided escalating military aid despite **Ngo Dinh Diem's administrative failures**. Resistance to the **Strategic Hamlet Program** alienated peasants, culminating in the US-backed military coup and Diem's removal in 1963.

topics.title: Escalation under Johnson and the Gulf of Tonkin
points: **The causes of conflict escalation and expanded US deployment, including the Vietcong threat and the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident.**
topics.narrative_blurb: President Johnson escalated direct military deployment to counter the growing **Vietcong threat** in the South. Exploiting the disputed **1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident**, Johnson secured the Tonkin Resolution from Congress, initiating sustained bombing raids in Operation Rolling Thunder and deploying the first official US ground combat troops to Da Nang in March 1965.

topics.title: Nature of Conflict: Tactics and Guerrilla Warfare
points: **US military tactics, including Operation Rolling Thunder, search-and-destroy missions, and the use of chemical defoliants.**
**The guerrilla warfare strategies utilized by the Vietcong forces.**
topics.narrative_blurb: The conflict pitted asymmetric doctrines against each other. The communist NLF utilized elusive **guerrilla warfare strategies**, including the Ho Chi Minh Trail, booby traps, and complex underground tunnels. The US military countered with industrial firepower: **Operation Rolling Thunder, search-and-destroy missions**, helicopter mobility, and the devastating **use of chemical defoliants** like Agent Orange and napalm.

topics.title: The Tet Offensive (1968) and Its Impact
points: **The main features and historical significance of the 1968 Tet Offensive.**
**The psychological impact on the US public and the credibility gap.**
topics.narrative_blurb: In January 1968, communist forces launched the massive **1968 Tet Offensive**, assaulting over 100 cities. Though an American military victory, television coverage shattered official optimism, widening an unbridgeable 'credibility gap'. The psychological shock convinced Walter Cronkite the war was unwinnable, directly influencing President Johnson's decision not to seek re-election.

sections.title: Key topic 4: Reactions to, and the end of, US involvement in the Vietnam War, 1964–75

topics.title: Reasons for the Growth of Opposition to the War
points: **Factors behind the rise of anti-war opposition, including the military draft and televised media reports.**
**The public response to the My Lai Massacre (1968) and its exposure.**
**The campus anti-war movement and the 1970 Kent State University shootings.**
topics.narrative_blurb: Domestic opposition surged due to **the military draft and televised media reports** bringing graphic casualties into living rooms. Moral outrage erupted worldwide with **the public response to the My Lai Massacre (1968) and its exposure**. Student radicalism peaked on university campuses, culminating in tragedy during the **1970 Kent State University shootings** by Ohio National Guardsmen.

topics.title: Nixon's Policies: Vietnamization and Widening War
points: **The core components of the Vietnamisation policy.**
**Military incursions into Cambodia (1970) and Laos (1971), and the 1972 air campaigns over North Vietnam.**
**The concept of the silent majority.**
topics.narrative_blurb: President Richard Nixon introduced **the Vietnamisation policy** to withdraw ground troops while training the ARVN. Appealing to the patriotic **silent majority**, Nixon simultaneously expanded aerial warfare through controversial **military incursions into Cambodia (1970) and Laos (1971)**, punctuated by the massive **1972 air campaigns over North Vietnam** (Operation Linebacker) to halt communist offensives.

topics.title: Peace Negotiations and the 1973 Paris Accords
points: **The motivations and main elements of the peace negotiations between 1972 and 1973.**
**The historical significance and terms of the 1973 Paris Peace Agreement.**
topics.narrative_blurb: Diplomatic pressure orchestrated through **peace negotiations between 1972 and 1973** by Henry Kissinger and Le Duc Tho produced a breakthrough following the 'Christmas Bombings'. The **terms of the 1973 Paris Peace Agreement** mandated the complete withdrawal of all US military personnel and the release of American prisoners of war, ending direct US combat involvement.

topics.title: The Fall of Saigon and the Legacy of the War
points: **The collapse of South Vietnamese resistance and the fall of Saigon (1975).**
**The human casualties and financial costs of the Vietnam War for the United States.**
topics.narrative_blurb: Without American air support, South Vietnamese forces disintegrated before North Vietnam's conventional 1975 offensive, culminating in the traumatic **fall of Saigon (1975)**. The war inflicted staggering **human casualties and financial costs for the United States**, claiming over 58,000 American lives, draining $167 billion, and shattering the post-war consensus of American military invincibility.
